saints.name: Sts. Perpetua and Felicity
saints.title: Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: A young noblewoman and her slave companion who went joyfully to the beasts at Carthage, leaving one of the earliest first-person accounts of martyrdom…
biography: In 203, during the persecution of Septimius Severus, five catechumens were arrested at Carthage: Vibia Perpetua, a well-born matron of twenty-two with an infant son at her breast; the slaves Felicity and Revocatus; and Saturninus and Secundulus. Their catechist Saturus gave himself up to join them.

In prison Perpetua wrote down her visions and the tears of her pagan father, who came repeatedly to beg her to sacrifice. Felicity, eight months with child, was delivered of a daughter two days before the games, lest she be left behind when her companions went to their death.

On 7 March they were exposed to the beasts at the games held for the birthday of Caesar Geta: the men were torn by leopards and bears, the women tossed by a maddened cow, and all were dispatched by the sword, Perpetua herself steadying the young gladiator's shaking blade to her throat.

The "Passion of Perpetua and Felicity," which preserves her diary, is among the earliest surviving Christian writings by a woman, and their names stand together in the Roman Canon of the Mass. Because one nursed her child and the other gave birth in chains, they are patrons of mothers and expectant mothers.
saints.knownFor: Their courage and the ancient “Passion” that records it.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 6 March
